## liboqs

### 0.17 essentials

The 0.17 project board lists five essential items: disabling Classic McEliece by default ([PR #2640](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2640), merged October 29) and the four remaining round 3 signature algorithms. QR-UOV was merged last week, and SDitH ([PR #2586](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2586)) was merged on October 30. Rodrigo thanked Owen and Bruce for their work on SDitH. ### SQIsign ([PR #2593](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2593))

Basil has addressed the review comments. Rodrigo had suggested further deduplication of header files, as he had for QR-UOV, but agreed with Michael that any such work should come after the algorithm is merged. The PR touches about 289 files, which Rodrigo considers fine as it is. He also noted Bruce's earlier point that deduplication is not always worth the review effort and complexity it adds, so it should not be taken for granted. Michael added that deferring further work until after merging also keeps the other integrations, in particular FAEST, from becoming more complicated, and supports merging SQIsign as it is. Basil said the PR already moves shared code into a common folder, and that perhaps four or five small files could still be deduplicated. He would also leave that for a follow-up.

The only other open item is switching the import URL to the official upstream repository. The SQIsign team still has to merge Basil's upstream change and push it to their public repository. Luca has looked at it, but someone else on the team should also review it, which Basil expects within a week or two. Rodrigo said this should not block the PR, since QR-UOV was also merged from Orlando's repository before the official upstream was available. Basil agreed, and the URL can be changed before the release.

The PR is ready for review. Rodrigo has reviewed it and is happy with it, but a second reviewer is needed. Bruce had volunteered, and anyone else is welcome to take it on. Michael pointed out that Basil's latest rebase dismissed Rodrigo's approval, so Rodrigo will re-review.

### HQC update ([issue #2670](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2670))

Before the meeting, Douglas asked whether liboqs 0.17 should include the updated HQC implementation (specification of 2026-10-12). He became aware of it that morning through a new Internet-Draft proposing HQC code points for TLS, for which he opened an oqs-provider issue ([issue #867](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/867)). He had Claude do a trial update by rerunning `copy_from_upstream`. It worked, and although the result needs a careful review, the update looks plausible and not too difficult. Rodrigo said HQC is an important algorithm whose standard will probably be published soon, so it is worth doing if it can be done at a good pace. Michael said `copy_from_upstream` has proven reliable and the update should be straightforward, so it should go on the list.

Owen asked whether to also add the x86-optimized HQC implementations ([issue #2481](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2481)). Rodrigo thought this would be less trivial and should not take time away from round 3. Michael considers round 3 essentially done apart from review, so there is room for more. Douglas pointed out that nobody yet knows where the optimizations are. For example, they might include an optimized AES that would have to be swapped for liboqs's common code. Michael noted there is precedent for not always doing that. Douglas suggested seeing how the version update goes before committing to the optimized code.

Agreed: updating HQC is treated as high priority (low effort, high reward), and the x86-optimized implementations will be considered afterwards, at a lower priority.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Douglas):** Push the HQC update as a PR; Douglas and Bruce to review.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Rodrigo):** Add the HQC update to the 0.17 project board.

### CI runtime ([issue #2658](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2658))

Michael raised the CI runtime, which has grown again. He would like the group to agree on how long CI should take. Time budgets were defined earlier, but the project has not kept to them, and the long runs slow development down. He proposed reserving thorough testing for two occasions, runs triggered manually by a maintainer and the weekly runs, and skipping leak testing for the long-running algorithms on pushes and PRs. Rodrigo said this sounded agreeable, since something similar has been done in oqs-provider. A few weeks ago he reduced liboqs CI to about 25 minutes; it is now about 70.

[PR #2667](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2667) gated the slow MQOM and QR-UOV leak tests out of PR runs. A commit Douglas then added to harden the gating raised the PR's runtime from about 50 to over 70 minutes. That commit re-enabled the tests on pushes and widened the set of paths that trigger them to code that is shared, but changed often. By Michael's analysis, the tests now run about three times as often. Michael merged PR #2667 as an interim step and has set out his reasoning on the issue. Rodrigo noted that part of the growth comes from the new algorithms. Michael agreed, but said tests are being run over and over on code that has not changed. Douglas will comment on the issue.

Michael proposed adding a time limit to the CI workflows. A hard stop would make the problem obvious but would lose the results of the run. A soft stop would be a background step that raises a warning or error once the budget is exceeded, while the rest of the run completes. Rodrigo preferred the soft stop, but wants a concise proposal agreed on the issue first.

Later in the meeting, Owen suggested starting from what each CI stage is meant to achieve (each push, each PR, each merge to `main`) and working backwards to how long each takes, rather than setting a budget in minutes and fitting tests into it. Michael welcomed the structured approach but stressed that the result still has to stay within the time limit, using parallelism where needed. He asked everyone to comment on the issue.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Douglas):** Comment on [issue #2658](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2658) about the leak-test gating added to PR #2667.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (all):** Comment on [issue #2658](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/issues/2658) on the goals of each CI stage and on a soft or hard time limit.

## OQS-OpenSSL 3 provider

**Code point assignment ([PR #852](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/852)).** Rodrigo dismissed an earlier approval after addressing one of the review comments, and thinks the PR is now good to go. As explained last week, the PR changes how code points are assigned. It is essential for adding the round 3 algorithms, since the provider would otherwise run out of code points.

**Round 3 algorithms.** Rodrigo had planned to add QR-UOV and SDitH in separate PRs once PR #852 lands. Michael preferred a single PR, since each extra PR means another review, and the remaining algorithms are close to landing in liboqs. Agreed: once all round 3 algorithms are in liboqs, Rodrigo will add them to the provider in one PR, and he will close the QR-UOV PR ([PR #849](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/849)).
